Worked Example: From the Last Period

Doctors count pregnancy from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP), and a full pregnancy is counted as 40 weeks, or 280 days. If your LMP was January 10, 2026, your estimated due date is October 17, 2026 (LMP + 280 days, often called Naegele's rule).

Why Your Date Can Change

  • Naegele's rule assumes a 28-day cycle with ovulation on day 14. With longer or shorter cycles, the date shifts.
  • An early ultrasound measures the fetus and may move the date if it differs from the LMP date by more than a few days.
  • IVF pregnancies use the embryo transfer date, which is precise.

The Due Date Is an Estimate

Only a small share of babies are born on the exact due date. ACOG describes 39 weeks to 40 weeks 6 days as full term, so a birth two weeks either side of the date is normal. Track your week-by-week progress with the pregnancy calculator, and see the likely conception window.

extra_faqs.q: How accurate is a due date?
extra_faqs.a: It is an estimate. Most births happen within a couple of weeks of the date. Your provider may adjust it after an early ultrasound.

extra_faqs.q: What if my cycle is not 28 days?
extra_faqs.a: Enter your actual cycle length if the calculator offers it. Longer cycles usually mean later ovulation and a later due date.

extra_faqs.q: When is a baby considered full term?
extra_faqs.a: ACOG defines full term as 39 weeks 0 days through 40 weeks 6 days.
